facts.title: Predicted Before It Was Found
facts.text: Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap below iodine in his periodic table and called the missing element 'eka-iodine,' predicting a heavy halogen would eventually fill it. For decades chemists hunted for this element in nature, but every claimed discovery turned out to be a mistake. The real element finally arrived in 1940 by creating it artificially rather than finding it in a mineral.

facts.title: Born in a Berkeley Cyclotron
facts.text: Astatine was first synthesized in 1940 by Dale Corson, Kenneth MacKenzie, and Emilio Segre at the University of California, Berkeley. They bombarded bismuth-209 with alpha particles in a cyclotron, producing astatine-211 through a nuclear reaction. This made it one of the first elements created by humans rather than discovered in rocks or minerals.

facts.title: A Name Meaning 'Unstable'
facts.text: The element's name comes from the Greek word 'astatos,' meaning unstable, a fitting label for one of the most radioactive elements known. Every single isotope of astatine is radioactive, with none being stable. The name was officially adopted in 1947, capturing the defining feature that no atom of it lasts very long.

facts.title: The Rarest Natural Element on Earth
facts.text: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, with estimates suggesting less than 30 grams exist worldwide at any moment. It forms continuously as a fleeting product in the decay chains of uranium and thorium, only to vanish almost immediately. If you could gather every natural astatine atom on the planet, it would not fill a teaspoon.

facts.title: A Few-Hour Lifetime at Best
facts.text: The longest-lived isotope, astatine-210, has a half-life of only about 8.1 hours, while the medically useful astatine-211 lasts roughly 7.2 hours. Many other isotopes survive for mere seconds or fractions of a second. This extreme instability means astatine cannot be stockpiled and must be produced fresh and used quickly.

facts.title: Nobody Has Ever Seen It
facts.text: Astatine is so radioactive that a visible, weighable sample can never be assembled, because its own intense radiation would instantly vaporize any lump through the heat it generates. Scientists study it only in vanishingly tiny, invisible quantities containing far fewer than a billionth of a gram. As a result, no human has ever actually seen pure astatine with their own eyes, and its exact appearance is unknown.

facts.title: The Metallic Halogen
facts.text: Although astatine sits among the halogens with fluorine, chlorine, and iodine, it behaves in surprisingly metallic ways as the heaviest member of the group. Chemists predict it would look dark or even shiny like a metalloid rather than a colorful gas or solid. Some of its chemistry resembles a metal, showing how elements can shift character as they grow heavier down a column.

facts.title: A Cancer-Targeting Bullet
facts.text: Astatine-211 is studied for targeted alpha-particle therapy, a promising cancer treatment that attaches the isotope to molecules which seek out tumor cells. When astatine-211 decays it releases alpha particles that travel only a few cell-widths, destroying cancer cells while largely sparing healthy tissue nearby. This short range makes it a precise tool against small tumors and scattered cancer cells.

facts.title: Made One Atom at a Time
facts.text: Producing astatine-211 for research requires a particle accelerator to bombard bismuth targets with high-energy alpha particles, a process only a handful of facilities worldwide can perform. The yields are so small that scientists often work with quantities measured in billionths of a gram. This scarcity and difficulty of production remain major hurdles to using astatine in widespread medicine.

facts.title: Thyroid Cousin of Iodine
facts.text: Because astatine is a halogen like iodine, the human thyroid gland tends to absorb it, just as it collects iodine from food. This behavior interests medical researchers, since it could allow astatine-211 to be delivered to the thyroid for treating certain cancers. The same chemical family relationship that defines its place on the periodic table also shapes how it interacts with the body.
